ch10.d.rA: Distance of both masses from the axis on rotor A
ch10.d.rB: Distance of both masses from the axis on rotor B
ch10.d.m: Mass of each of the four masses on the rods
ch10.d.tau: Constant torque applied equally to both rotors
ch10.d.shape: Ring, disk and rod with the same mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m (rod 1 m long)
ch10.d.d: Distance from the centre of mass to the rotation axis; drag the axis ⊙
ch10.r.goal.I: Rotational inertia $I = \sum m r^2$ depends on how the mass is spread around the axis, not only on the mass
ch10.r.goal.alpha: With the same torque, a larger $I$ gives a smaller angular acceleration $\alpha = \tau/I$
ch10.r.obs.four: Default $r_B = 2r_A$: the bars show $I_B = 4I_A$; each mass contributes $mr^2$, four times as much
ch10.r.obs.slope: The slope of $\omega(t)$ is $\alpha$: B's slope is a quarter of A's
ch10.r.assume: Massless rods and axles, point masses, frictionless axles, seen from above
ch10.pa.goal.theorem: Parallel-axis theorem: about an axis parallel to one through the centre of mass, a distance $d$ away, $I = I_\text{cm} + Md^2$
ch10.pa.goal.shape: $I_\text{cm}$ depends on the shape; the $Md^2$ term does not
ch10.pa.obs.drag: Drag the axis (⊙): the point on the graph follows the parabola $I(d)$
ch10.pa.obs.min: $I$ is smallest at $d = 0$, the axis through the centre of mass (⊕)
ch10.pa.obs.same: Changing the body only shifts the parabola up or down; its curvature ($M$) is the same
ch10.pa.obs.order: $I_\text{cm}$: ring $MR^2$ > disk $\tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$ > rod $\tfrac{1}{12}M(2R)^2 = \tfrac{1}{3}MR^2$; the farther the mass from the axis, the larger
ch10.pa.assume: Thin ring, uniform disk and rod; the axis is perpendicular to the page
